name: F-Pattern (Reading)
description: Users scan web content in a rough F-shaped pattern: two horizontal sweeps across the top of the content area, then a vertical scan down the left side, reading progressively less as they go.
design_relevance_note: Frequently cited to justify front-loading the most important words/content at the start of headlines, paragraphs, and left-aligned page structure — the basis for 'put your keywords first' content-design guidance.
myth_risk_note: Updated 2026-09-07: myth risk stays moderate rather than dropping to low, because even with real backing for the narrower text-page claim, the F-pattern is still widely invoked in design practice as a universal scanning law for all web content -- exactly the overgeneralization this entry's own confirmed evidence contradicts.
prevalence_note: One of the most frequently cited claims in UX writing and content-design practice specifically — taught throughout NN/G's own extensive canon and referenced across countless style guides and content-strategy curricula as the basis for 'front-load your headlines' guidance. Excluded from this taxonomy in an earlier extraction batch on backing_status grounds alone before Jose flagged that prevalence, not just rigor, should drive inclusion — see docs/SCHEMA.md's 'Why prevalence exists' section.

findings.description: Nielsen's F-pattern eye-tracking scan path was directly confirmed in both text-browsing and text-searching tasks on a real e-commerce web page. However, on an image-based version of the same page, users did not follow the F-pattern at all -- browsing produced a uniform scan path weighted toward above-the-fold images, and searching produced unique, efficient, non-F-shaped paths. The pattern is real, but narrower than its popular design-practice framing as a universal web-reading law: it holds for text-heavy pages, not image-heavy ones.
findings.effect_size: Qualitative confirmation of scan-path shape (eye-tracking), not a single numeric effect size
findings.source_title: “F” Pattern Scanning of Text and Images in Web Pages
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting

applications.title: NN/g eyetracking studies confirm F-shaped scanning on real sites (TigersInCrisis.com, History.com)
applications.description: NN/g's 2006 and 2017 eyetracking studies recorded aggregate gaze heatmaps from dozens of participants reading unformatted, prose-heavy pages on TigersInCrisis.com (looking up Sumatran tiger population figures) and an earlier History.com page (about the 1900 Galveston flood); both produced the characteristic F-shaped concentration of fixations along the top and left of the content area, confirming the pattern persists across an 11-year replication gap and on both desktop and mobile.
applications.ethical_note: This is a descriptive finding about human reading behavior on unformatted text, not a technique anyone is deploying to influence users -- there is no manipulator here, just an attentional pattern that well-formatted content can work with or against. Graded not_applicable rather than user_beneficial or manipulative because doing so would imply an intentional actor exploiting the pattern, when the actual finding concerns default reading behavior in the absence of any formatting decisions at all.
